exercise.title: Two eras, three mechanisms: regular sound change, name avoidance, and borrowed garment terms
exercise.fiction_notice: All forms, names, roles, objects, dates, and rules below are invented design variables for a fictional world. Nothing here is a real language, rite, law, or historical event; no real ritual material is copied or reconstructed.
exercise.people: Invented communities: 'Old Maru' speakers (Era I) and 'Late Maru' speakers (Era II); invented 'Sedrin' donor traders supply two loan strata.

eras.label: Old Maru
eras.language_state: Laws L1-L4 productive in years 40-120; proto forms still transparent.

eras.label: Late Maru
eras.language_state: L1-L4 inert; native forms now show the outcomes; loans can arrive with unshifted donor phonology.
registers: recitation register (frozen Old Maru memorized form)

symbol_readings.constraint: Readings are role- and era-bound; the same motif can be re-read in a later era, and one audience's reading is not evidence for another's. No universal one-symbol-one-domain mapping is asserted by this exercise.

era_staging.note: Dates are invented; era labels describe in-world political/language stages, not real periods.

design_assumptions: Toy forward calendar; years 40-120 are the only window in which L1-L4 are productive.
L1-L4 are exceptionless in their stated environments; apparent exceptions must be loans, learned channels, or analogy, and are not modeled here.
Loans enter from one donor variety through one channel per stratum; dialect mixture is excluded by assumption.
The avoidance rule targets a referent's designation, not a sound sequence; homophones of the avoided form survive (D9).
The recitation register is a memorized frozen form; its retention of aku and kalu does not prove that everyday speech kept them.
Every dated witness is invented; the exercise shows method, not history.

lore_handoff.status: proposal only; canon decisions are never made in this exercise
limits: Non-canon: all forms, dates, roles, and rules are design variables.
Hand off law lists, strata tables, and the avoidance ledger as options with confidence grades, not as world facts.
Do not copy any real ritual, oath, or restricted text into the world bible on the strength of this exercise.
The real-source audits below support method choices only; they do not license naming or dressing any real community's practice.
In-world disputes (is har one etymon or two?) should remain open; the merged forms kalu and haru are indistinguishable in Era II.
open_questions: Which era is canonical for the roll of year 95 vs the inventory of year 352, if authored?
Does the mourning-year rule extend to the common noun haru in any later era (would break D9's contrast)?
Is the apika reborrowing a court fashion or a market term (two different diffusion stories)?

audits.claim: The Germanic words for 'bear' are conventionally explained as an avoidance substitution for the older inherited animal name, parallel to Russian medved' 'honey-eater'.
audits.source_locator: Etymology notes, paragraph 2 of the noun 'bear' section
audits.source_excerpt: the Germanic languages replaced the older name of the bear, *h₂ŕ̥tḱos, with the epithet 'brown one', presumably due to taboo avoidance; compare Russian медве́дь
audits.basis: coupling language+myth - retrieved full text states the replacement and the avoidance motivation; a second retrieval (медведь) independently confirms the 'honey-eater' gloss. The motivation wording is 'presumably'; see audit-02.
audits.access_limit: Wiktionary is a public reference, not the handbook cited by the entry (Campbell 2013; Mallory & Adams 2006 not retrieved); no page numbers asserted.

audits.claim: Latin castra 'camp' is the etymon of English place-name elements -chester/-caster via Old English ceaster.
audits.source_locator: Etymology (English section, first line); the Latin link restated in the downstream-language section
audits.source_excerpt: From Middle English Chestre, from Old English Ċeaster, from ċeaster ('a town or city, especially a Roman one').
audits.basis: linguistic-strata bibliography fact - retrieved full text supports the Latin/OE/English chain; the second section of the same page glosses ceaster as 'a borrowing from Latin castrum (camp)'.
audits.access_limit: The -caster variant and the castra vs castrum form difference were not separately retrieved.

audits.claim: Under Chinese naming-taboo conventions, personal-name characters could receive substitutions (including similar-sounding ones), blanks, or stroke omission.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/synthesis/taboo-euphemism-lifecycle.md section 8, 'Symbolic system' row (cited there as W22)
audits.source_excerpt: Changing the character to another, usually a synonym or one which sounded similar to the character being avoided.
audits.basis: coupling language+era (naming institution) - retrieved article lists the same three methods (substitution incl. homophones, blank, stroke omission) and shows scoping rules (a Tang edict limited avoidance to two characters in direct succession), matching the entry's summary.
audits.access_limit: Reference-tier encyclopedia, not the entry's cited manual (W22 Wilkinson not retrievable; chinaknowledge.de returned 404/network failure). Institutional corroboration pending.
